Could Wednesday be the last 100° DAY!?!

THE FIRST FRONT IS ON THE WAY!

We’ve still got a few more days of serious September heat to get through, with highs near or above 100° through Wednesday. In fact, Wednesday could very well end up being our LAST 100° DAY OF THE YEAR. 🤞

Then comes the change.

Confidence continues to increase that a cold front will push into the area Wednesday evening into Thursday morning, bringing a much better chance for showers and thunderstorms along with noticeably cooler temperatures. Rain chances may linger into Friday. 

And here’s the part I really like: this may only be the first of several fronts. The overall pattern looks increasingly favorable for additional fronts and potentially even cooler air as we head toward the middle of September. 

So hang in there. We’re almost through this latest blast of summer.

Could Wednesday really be the last 100° day of 2026? I sure hope so!

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
What an incredible view from the Hurricane Hunters as they fly into the eye of major Hurricane Lowell!

That towering wall of white clouds surrounding the clear blue sky is the eyewall, the most vicious and destructive part of a hurricane, where the strongest winds and most intense weather are found. In a powerful hurricane, those thunderstorms can tower more than 50,000 feet into the atmosphere.

You can also see what’s known as the “stadium effect.” The eyewall slopes outward with height, making the view from inside the eye look like you’re standing on the field of a massive stadium with the clouds rising like walls all around you.

The fringe of Lowell is impacting the western islands of Hawaii including Kauai and Oahu with gusty winds and heavy rain today through Tuesday.

We’ve got spoons!!!! ❄️❄️❄️❄️

 Every fall I love seeing some of the old weather folklore start making the rounds, and this one is a classic.

According to folklore, if you cut open a locally grown persimmon seed, the shape inside can supposedly give us a hint about the winter ahead:

🥄 Spoon = lots of snow think “snow shovel”
🔪 Knife = bitter cold and cutting winds
🍴 Fork = a milder winter with lighter snow 

Well… take a look at these seeds. Those sure look like SPOONS to me! 🥄

So if you believe the old folklore, somebody might want to make sure the snow shovel is ready this winter. 

Is it scientific? Nope. Even climate researchers who have looked at the tradition say there isn’t evidence that the shape actually predicts the upcoming winter. 

But weather folklore is part of the fun of watching the seasons change.

What do you see 

spoon, knife or fork?

Half Moon Plumbing & Electric

*Big El Niño Boost in next few weeks! 
Our already record El Niño is about to get a spike to “Historic”. Humans have never seen such an event, so I’d expect some unprecedented events. 
A major push of west winds in the Tropical Pacific will surge warm water east. The result is a peak monthly #ElNino strength in November-December around +4.0° C above normal, breaking the old monthly record of +2.8°C in 2015. Pictured here is the US CFS (seasonal model) which is in lock step with the European model. The white shades indicating sea surface temps 5-7°C above average in November. 
For the US South and #Florida this means a strong subtropical jet stream will form by late fall, with frequent fronts, severe weather, and weekly rainfall - #California will also cash in on this extra rain come winter. @topfans

BREAKING: HURRICANE WATCH ISSUED FOR KAUAʻI AND NIʻIHAU HAWAII🚨Hurricane Lowell is moving north toward Hawaii, prompting officials to issue a Hurricane Watch for Kauaʻi County! This means hurricane conditions are now possible across Kauaʻi and Niʻihau. A Tropical Storm Warning also remains in effect, with conditions expected to deteriorate Monday afternoon or evening.

As of 5 PM HST Sunday, Lowell remained a Category 3 hurricane with sustained winds of 120 mph, located about 500 miles south-southwest of Līhuʻe. Lowell is expected to accelerate north to north-northeast and pass just west of the main Hawaiian Islands Monday night. Although weakening is forecast, Lowell should remain a hurricane during its closest approach.

Hurricane-force winds extend 60 miles from the center, while tropical-storm-force winds extend up to 175 miles. Terrain could enhance winds by 30% or more across Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, allowing some gusts to reach hurricane force. A small eastward shift in the track could significantly increase the wind threat.

Additional rainfall of 6-10 inches is forecast on Kauaʻi, with isolated totals up to 14 inches. Significant flash flooding and mudslides are possible. Coastal inundation of 1-3 feet, destructive surf and dangerous rip currents are also expected. Several tornadoes are possible near Kauaʻi and Niʻihau Monday afternoon through Monday night, with a lower tornado threat elsewhere across the islands.

Preparations on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau should be completed as soon as possible🌧️🌊💨

items.author: GregDeeWeather
items.text:
HAWAII | Sunce late last week, the NHC has updated & tweaked the storm forecast & adjusted some arrival times. 

Earlier it looked like tropical storm wind would reach Kauai County in western Hawaii by Labor Day morning, local time. Now it looks like that won’t happen until later in the afternoon. 

Some things to consider that you can still do through Monday morning:

⚠️Yard & Exterior

 * Clear the lānai: Patio furniture, gas grills, trash bins, umbrellas, and hanging orchid baskets become airborne surprisingly fast in 45-mph gusts. Bring them indoors or into a garage/shed; don't just push them against an exterior wall.

 * Trim heavy foliage and harvest early: Cut dead palm fronds, thin out heavy banana stalks, and harvest heavy fruits (coconuts, breadfruit, papayas) near windows, parked cars, or power drops. High trade or tropical winds snap heavy branches easily.

 * Secure solar panels and loose roofing: Check for loose corrugated metal sheets, flashing, or solar array mounts. At 50 mph, wind can catch the undersides of unanchored panels or loose sheet-metal overhangs.

⚠️Windows & Water Intrusion

 * Crank and latch jalousie (louvered) windows: Common across older island single-wall homes, jalousies leak wind-driven rain heavily. Ensure every louver is fully turned tight, inspect rubber gaskets, and wedge towels along sills to catch water.

 * Brace sliding glass doors: High winds exert significant lateral pressure on large glass tracks. Place a wooden dowel or security bar in the slider channel to prevent the door from rattling or popping off its track.

 * Clear gutters and downspouts: Tropical storms bring intense bursts of rain alongside wind. Clogged roof drains and ʻauwai (drainage ditches) back up quickly, causing overflow into eaves and foundations.

⚠️Island-Specific Infrastructure

 * Catchment system prep: If your property relies on rainwater harvesting, disconnect the downspout diverter before the storm hits. Strong winds blow salt spray, bird droppings, and loose vegetative debris onto the roof, which will contaminate your holding tank if washed in.

 * Prep for localized power cuts: Tree limbs on overhead lines are the primary cause of outages at this wind tier. Charge portable power banks, test flashlights, and verify that solar-battery backup systems or backup generators have fuel and are clear of standing water.

 * Account for local microclimates: Depending on your location relative to the mountains (e.g., Pali corridors, gulches, or downslope leeward areas), local terrain can funnel and accelerate 40-mph regional winds into 60+ mph localized gusts. Take extra care if your property sits in a known wind-venturi channel.

items.author: EricGravesWX
items.text:
Should really, really read this if you dealt with, or plan to deal with a tropical system in the future.
   This is something 99% of the population isn't aware of when it comes to "sustained wind speeds", and quick "gusts" in hurricanes, and it's probably going to be opposite of what you thought.
    When you see a hurricane with "sustained" winds of 130 mph making landfall, you will be very hard pressed to even find "gusts" that are near those high "sustained, 60 second average" wind speeds found by Hurricane Hunter Aircraft. 
   Those sustained speeds are found over the ocean, well away from land, 30 feet above the ocean, and they search for a while to find that high number. 
   Basically, a good rule of thumb is, the quick "gusts" measured along the beach (on land) will usually only match, or even be a bit less than what the Hurricane Hunter Aircraft finds as a sustained 1 minute average wind speed. Just look up Andrew top gusts, Laura, Delta, Rita, Ike, Ian etc.
   With that being said, when it came to "Tropical Storm" Edouard, many gusts were found in the 70 to 80 mph range.....about what you would find in a category 1 hurricane.

items.author: maxvelocitywx
items.text:
The CFS model is already going bullish on a potentially snowy winter across the Southern & Eastern United States...

The newest run depicts a strongly El Niño-like winter pattern, though September climate model forecasts remain highly uncertain and should be taken with a very heavy grain of salt. The model projects below-average snowfall across the Pacific Northwest and Great Lakes, alongside above-average snowfall stretching from the southern Plains into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

Long-range snowfall forecasts this far in advance have very limited skill and cannot reliably anticipate shorter-term winter drivers, including sudden stratospheric warming events and the eventual extent of Eurasian snow cover (especially across Siberia). Additionally, individual model runs can fluctuate significantly from run to run.

That said, this particular pattern is broadly consistent with what we'd expect from a strong El Niño. During strong El Niño events, the subtropical jet typically shifts southward and extends eastward, favoring increased moisture and storm activity across the southern tier of the United States. This storm track historically favors below-average snowfall across portions of the northern United States, particularly the Pacific Northwest and Great Lakes, while increasing precipitation and the potential for significant snowfall farther south and along the East Coast.

One important thing to note: this is a model signal, not a winter forecast. Current guidance strongly favors a very strong El Niño this winter, which does increase confidence in the broad-scale pattern, but the eventual snowfall distribution will depend heavily on shorter-term atmospheric patterns that cannot be predicted with much confidence in early September.

items.author: MikeCollierWx
items.text:
WINTER LOVERS… this is getting interesting.

It’s only early September, so there is a LONG way to go before winter, but the early signals continue to catch my attention.

Two different seasonal models, the CFSv2 and CanSIPS, are currently showing above normal snowfall across parts of Oklahoma and the central/southern Plains this winter. The CFSv2 signal is particularly impressive, with the above normal snowfall corridor extending from the southern Plains through the Tennessee/Ohio Valley and into the Northeast.

Now, nobody should look at a September seasonal model and start measuring the kids for snow boots. These forecasts will change many times between now and December.

But here’s what has my attention: we continue to see multiple pieces of guidance leaning toward a potentially more active winter across our part of the country.

There’s also a fascinating wrinkle developing with the Pacific pattern. If we end up with a stronger El Niño while the PDO remains negative, we don’t have a nice collection of historical winters that perfectly matches what we’re seeing. That makes simply grabbing an old El Niño winter and calling it an “analog” much less useful.

So no, I’m definitely not forecasting specific snowfall totals in September.

But am I becoming increasingly interested in the possibility of more snow than normal in Oklahoma this winter?

Absolutely.

Winter lovers, you have my attention. 👀

HAWAII TROPICAL STORM WARNING ISSUED‼️🌀🌧️a Tropical Storm Warning is now in effect for Kauai and Niihau as powerful Hurricane Lowell begins turning north toward the Hawaiian Islands. Tropical storm-force winds are possible across Kauai County Monday into Tuesday.

As of this morning, Lowell remains a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 125 mph,
located roughly 580 miles south-southwest of Kauai. The hurricane is expected to accelerate north and eventually north-northeast, passing roughly 100-200 miles west of Kauai Monday night while gradually weakening.

🌧️Even without a direct landfall, significant impacts are expected across Hawaii. Heavy rain and flooding likely. Tropical moisture is already increasing across the islands, and the threat will ramp up through tonight and Monday. A Flood Watch is in effect statewide through Tuesday, with the greatest flooding risk from this afternoon through Tuesday morning. Heavy rain and thunderstorms could produce flash flooding, rapidly rising streams and mudslides. Kauai and Niihau are expected to see some of the highest rainfall totals, but flooding is possible across the entire island chain🌧️

🌬️Strong winds likely. Kauai and Niihau will experience the greatest wind threat with tropical storm-force winds of 39 mph or higher, possibly stronger if Lowell tracks slightly farther east🌬️

🌊Dangerous surf with very large swells generated by Lowell are already affecting Hawaii and will build substantially Monday. Surf could reach 18-22 feet along south-facing shores of Kauai Monday afternoon, with very large and potentially life-threatening surf also affecting west-facing shores of Kauai and south-west-facing shores of Oahu. Coastal flooding, beach erosion and dangerous rip currents are possible🌊

🌪️There is also a low but notable risk of brief tornadoes or waterspouts near Kauai and Niihau Monday, potentially embedded within Lowell's outer rain bands 🌪️

The center of Lowell is currently forecast to remain offshore, but this is a large and powerful hurricane. Small changes in its track could significantly change the wind, rain and coastal impacts,
particularly for Kauai and Niihau. Residents and visitors across Hawaii should closely monitor updates through Monday as Lowell makes its closest approach🌀‼️

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
NOT HEAT LIGHTNING

How crazy was all that lightning last night?!  It was continuous for hours, and based on all the videos I’ve received, many of you witnessed an amazing light show.  

There were more than 45,000 lightning strikes in this map view but within the red oval where that huge cluster of storms was, there was over 13,400 strikes over 6 hours.  

It wasn’t “heat lightning.” There were big thunderstorms about 35–40 miles offshore, but thunder can typically only be heard from about 10–15 miles away because the sound waves weaken and dissipate as they travel. So you could easily see the lightning without ever hearing the thunder.

So why was there so much lightning? Yesterday’s very hot and humid conditions gave the storms plenty of moisture and instability, fueling powerful updrafts. Those updrafts caused more collisions between ice and graupel (soft hail) high in the storms, building electrical charge and producing a ton of lightning.

Above-average temperatures are expected across the northern tier, extending from the Pacific Northwest through the Great Lakes and Northeast.

Below-average temperatures are favored across the southern tier, spanning from the Southwest through Texas and the Gulf Coast, although these wouldn't necessarily be spawned from polar vortexes, but rather persistent cloud cover and constant storms across the region.

Equal chances for above or below-average temperatures exist for regions in the central Plains, Mid-Atlantic, and central West Coast. Temperature swings from one way to another will be likely here.

DFW’s 100° Average Is Trending Up! ☀️🔥

DFW’s current official 30-year average (1991–2020) is 20 days of 100°+ temperatures per year.

Every 10 years, that 30-year average is updated. Currently 1991-2020. The next one will cover 2001–2030.

So far, through 2026, DFW is running at roughly 23 days per year. If we finish this summer with 50 days at 100°+, DFW would only need to average about 22 days per year from 2027–2030 for the new 30-year average to finish at 23 days per year.

🔥 Bottom line: When the new climate averages come out in 2031, there’s a good chance DFW’s average number of 100° days will be higher than today’s 20 days. 

And remember we still have four more summers after this one before that new 30 year average is finalized.

I’ve had lots of questions about averages. I would expect a lot of “above averages” until the new average resets in 2031.

items.author: ncweatherauthority
items.text:
Today marks the 30th anniversary of Hurricane Fran; on the evening of September 5th, 1996, at 830PM, Hurricane Fran made landfall near Bald Head Island. It left devastating impacts on NC; Fran developed from a Tropical wave that came off Africa and tracked across the Atlantic Ocean. Fran made landfall near Bald Head Island as a Cat 3 Hurricane with winds of 115MPH. Fran caused catastrophic damage and flooding; it was responsible for 26 deaths and was the most expensive natural disaster in NC ever at the time. Hurricane Fran brought impacts far inland with hurricane-force wind gusts into Raleigh. I spoke to some folks this month in Raleigh who remember it vividly; parts of Central North Carolina including Raleigh did not have power or running water for 1-3 weeks. It caused 4 billion dollars in damage with 750 million in the Raleigh/Wake County area alone. It remains one of the worst hurricanes to ever hit NC. A Wind gust of 105MPH occurred in Southport, a 100MPH Wind gust in Atlantic Beach, and a 79MPH wind gust in Raleigh. Fran’s easterly winds pushed a surge of water up the river basins. The storm surge reached 10 feet in Swansboro and along the Neuse River in New Bern. In Washington, the 9-foot surge up the Pamlico River. It caused a 12 foot surge along New Hanover and Pender County beaches. Parts of the state were without power for weeks, and some places were uninhabitable for months. Do you remember?

Raleigh's population has more than doubled since Hurricane Fran, and I can tell you from experience Raleigh is not ready for another major Hurricane by any means. When people ask if Hurricanes impact inland North Carolina, yes they do!  
-Ethan

LOWELL BEGINNING NORTH TURN | IMPACTS ON THE WAY FOR HAWAII🌀🌧️🌊Hurricane Lowell remains a powerful Category 4 Hurricane with sustained winds of 145 mph and gusts of 175 mph. Lowell looks to pass roughly 100-200 miles west of Kauai County Monday night, likely near Major-Hurricane strength.

Conditions will begin deteriorating Sunday afternoon and evening as deep tropical moisture spreads across the islands. Periods of heavy rain and thunderstorms may continue through Tuesday morning - and potentially into Wednesday - with flash flooding and mudslides possible statewide. Rainfall totals of 3-6 inches are forecast for Kauai and the Big Island, with localized amounts exceeding 10 inches possible. Strong southeast-to-south winds will also develop, especially across Kauai County, where tropical-storm conditions are possible late Monday or Monday night.

Dangerous surf will rapidly build along south-and west-facing shores, potentially becoming very large and destructive Monday. Combined with monthly high tides, coastal flooding could affect roads, properties, harbors and channels. Even though Lowell’s center is forecast to remain west of the main islands, impacts will extend hundreds of miles from the hurricane. Small track changes could significantly alter the severity of conditions, especially around Kauai🌀

HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE HEADING INTO THE WEST🌀🌧️Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture will still influence parts of the West this weekend, with another potentially broader surge possible next week.

The first push of moisture is already being drawn northeast ahead of a West Coast trough. Southern California will see increasing rain chances through Sunday, with generally light rainfall but locally heavier amounts around the mountains and foothills. A few thunderstorms are possible, and heavier showers could produce localized flooding.

By Sunday, the moisture plume stretches farther northeast across the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwest Arizona and Utah. Rain and thunderstorms will become more scattered farther east, but pockets of heavier rainfall will be possible, particularly from the Mojave Desert into southern Nevada and southwest Utah. Then attention turns to next week.

Marie is forecast to gradually weaken and turn more northwest to northward while remaining hundreds of miles offshore. Another Pacific trough could eventually capture some of Marie’s remnant tropical moisture and pull it northward along the West Coast and into the Great Basin during the middle to latter part of next week.

That could bring another increase in showers and thunderstorms across portions of California and Nevada, with some of that moisture potentially reaching Oregon and even the Pacific Northwest later in the week. Exactly how far north and inland the moisture gets remains uncertain and will depend heavily on the position of the next trough.

So again, while Marie is not forecast to make landfall in California, it's tropical moisture will get pulled away from the Hurricane in multiple waves. The first arrives this weekend, followed by the potential for a second and possibly broader surge next week. This does not mean it will rain everywhere or every day, but the overall pattern continues to favor periods of unusually deep moisture across portions of the West🌀🌧️

MORE STORMS POSSIBLE ACROSS THE NORTHWEST TODAY BUT COVERAGE LOOKS LESS THAN FRIDAY⛈️another round of showers and isolated thunderstorms is expected across portions of Washington, Oregon and Idaho this afternoon and evening as a cool upper-level low continues spinning over the Pacific Northwest. The Storm Prediction Center does have the entire region in a chance for thunderstorms but don't let that fool you, not everyone sees storms and most folks won't see storms.

If the atmosphere can recover from yesterday's storms, parts of Western Washington could be fairly active again this afternoon. Thunderstorms are expected to initially develop around the Cascades before some drift west toward the Puget Sound lowlands, similar to what happened Friday but, again, there are questions on how much destabilization occrus. Not everyone will see a storm, but lightning, locally heavy rain and gusty outflow winds will be possible underneath the stronger cells. Activity should gradually decrease around sunset.

Across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, scattered showers will redevelop with daytime heating, particularly around the Cascades and Coast Range. A few stronger, pulse-type thunderstorms could develop, capable of brief heavy rain, small hail, lightning and gusty-erratic winds.

Central and eastern Washington into northeast Oregon will also see scattered showers and a few thunderstorms. The Washington Cascades and northern Blue Mountains appear to have some of the better chances, although isolated activity is possible elsewhere. Instability is relatively weak, so widespread severe weather is not expected.

Around Bend and central Oregon, showers will remain possible as disturbances rotate around the upper low, with isolated thunderstorms mainly favoring the higher terrain. The overall setup continues to favor hit-or-miss rather than widespread storms. Southern Oregon will be quieter than yesterday with the best chances around the southern Oregon Cascades into northern Klamath County. Farther east, most of southwest Idaho should also be considerably drier today with only very isolated storms, mainly around eastern Valley County, Idaho, and western Baker County, Oregon.

If storms approach, move indoors and be especially careful if you're hiking or camping in the mountains. This is where storm coverage will be higher and lightning is likely⛈️

WIDESPREAD DAMAGING WINDS THIS AFTERNOON⚠️⛈️💨the severe weather risk is increasing this afternoon across parts of Virginia and the Carolinas, with the greatest concern across central and eastern North Carolina. The atmosphere is becoming very unstable, with thunderstorms strengthening and organizing as they move east. The primary risk is damaging wind gusts, and the Storm Prediction Center has increased severe wind probabilities across central/eastern North Carolina. A few of the strongest storms could also produce isolated large hail where the most intense updrafts occur.

Additional thunderstorms may redevelop farther west from parts of the Ohio Valley into the Tennessee Valley, where isolated damaging wind gusts will also be possible. Storms should gradually weaken this evening as daytime heating fades and the strongest activity moves toward the Atlantic coast. Have multiple ways to receive weather warnings, especially if you have outdoor plans this afternoon and evening⚠️⛈️💨

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is on pace to break the satellite-era record for the latest first hurricane...

None of the five tropical storms that have formed so far in 2026 have reached hurricane strength. The current record for the latest first hurricane is September 11, which was set in 2002 and tied in 2013. For reference, the historical average date for the first Atlantic hurricane is August 11.

With no new development expected in the near term, 2026 is highly likely to shatter this record as we head into the peak of the season.

items.author: NTXWC
items.text:
The STRONGEST El Niño EVER recorded is upon us, which will have SERIOUS effects on how our weather pattern plays out this winter.

An El Niño pattern happens when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become warmer than average.

This year, they are forecast to be the strongest we have *ever* seen. 

Strong El Niño winters typically feature a stronger, more active southern storm track, increasing the odds of wetter and sometimes cooler conditions across the southern U.S. 

That can mean more frequent storm systems crossing Texas and, when cold air is available, opportunities for winter storms, ice and snow. It does NOT guarantee a snowy winter, but an active subtropical jet gives us more systems capable of producing precipitation when cold air happens to be in place. 

A more active storm track means more storm energy for severe weather outbreaks as well. One unforgettable analog is the 2015-16 super El Niño. On December 26, 2015, North Texas experienced a major tornado outbreak producing 12 tornadoes, including the deadly Garland-Rowlett EF4. The outbreak killed 13 people. The 2015-16 El Niño was among the strongest on record.

Does this mean we will see widespread tornado outbreaks on the daily? Absolutely not. But going into an even stronger pattern than we've ever seen is certainly ringing alarm bells for a potentially anomalous winter across the southeast. 

Again, a strong El Niño does NOT mean tornadoes will strike your house, or a historic winter storm will dump buckets of snow on the southeast. There is no way to predict individual events. 

Think of it as potential energy storing up. This pattern will give us more storm track energy and opportunities to see frequent cold swings and severe weather outbreaks, but there is no saying in how, when, or where these specific events will play out. Only time will tell if the strongest El Niño will really live up to it's name.

HAWAII | In their latest update, the National Hurricane Center says that watches should be expected later today for western Hawaii ahead of Hurricane Lowell.

Though the eye of the storm will pass west of the islands, the large storm is now expected to be stronger as it passes west of the islands. This may help keep some of the strongest winds farther west, but it's likely that some level of tropical storm winds will be present on Kauai at least. Honolulu is likely to see rain squalls & heavy rains are possible all the way west to the Big Island, where strong southeast winds will bring in more tropical moisture. Higher elevations may get up to 10" of rain from the storm. 

The worst conditions are expected on Monday, Labor Day. 

 #hawaii #hurricane #lowell #kauai

Flash flooding is possible across parts of the coastal Mid-Atlantic!

A southward-pushing cold front will interact with an advancing upper-level wave and a moist airmass across the Mid-Atlantic and Carolina coastal plains this afternoon where high atmospheric moisture will support heavy rainfall rates of up to 2 inches per hour.

Storms interacting with the sea-breeze boundary could produce localized rainfall totals of 2 to 5 inches. While sandy soils along the coast can handle higher rainfall amounts, scattered incidents of rapid inundation and flash flooding remain possible.
